implementation_notes: Spring MVC is the canonical modern realization: DispatcherServlet is the front controller and dispatcher, HandlerMapping/HandlerAdapter locate and invoke the @Controller method (the worker), the method populates the Model and returns a logical view name or ModelAndView, and a ViewResolver (Thymeleaf, JSP, FreeMarker) renders it; @ControllerAdvice, filters and interceptors carry the cross-cutting work Front Controller used to do inline. What replaces the classic 2001 structure is the framework's front-controller machinery - you write workers, not a dispatcher. The servlet-front-controller variant remains the right choice when the deployment is a plain servlet container or dispatch policy must be bespoke.
pitfalls: Controllers are singletons: per-request state in a field leaks across concurrent requests - keep request data in method parameters or the model.
View names are strings resolved at request time, so a renamed template fails only when the request is served; assert resolution in a test or centralise view-name constants.
Business logic in the controller duplicates the service layer and breaks the layering this pattern assumes.

variants.name: Servlet front controller with Command helpers (classic J2EE form)
variants.implementation_notes: The classic form: one controller servlet mapped to a URL pattern delegates to a Command object obtained from a factory, the command executes application logic and returns a logical page name, and the controller forwards with getServletContext().getRequestDispatcher(page).forward(request, response); JavaBeans or custom tags hold the request-scoped model for the JSP view, and filters handle authentication and logging around the controller. Choose it when the deployment is a servlet container without Spring, or when dispatch semantics are genuinely custom; otherwise the framework variant costs far less code.
pitfalls: The command must not write to the response: once the response is committed, forward() throws IllegalStateException instead of rendering the view.
Request-scoped attributes are the model contract and are untyped - unchecked casts hide mismatches until the page renders.
JSPs stay directly reachable unless they live under WEB-INF or a security constraint blocks them, which bypasses the controller and every check it performs.
